995.title: Eisai
995.hook: brings Rinzai Zen and tea seeds back from China
995.howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen temples, tea is served as part of the daily schedule and at ceremonies, and the tea ceremony that later developed in Japan kept close ties to Zen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shinran's family, and a teacher who called himself neither monk nor layman. Your line was neither monk nor lay. Which ordinary moment did you treat as part of the path? Day nine hundred ninety-five.

The young shogun, in his capital at Kamakura, has a terrible morning after a night of drinking. Someone is sent for, and a Buddhist monk arrives carrying two things: a bowl of tea, and a little book he has written about tea and health. The shogun drinks, and, according to a chronicle of the time, feels better, and is pleased with the book. It is a small scene. But the monk carrying the bowl had brought home from China a lineage of Zen practice and, tradition says, the seeds of tea plants too. His name was Eisai.
screen: `A SHOGUN'S BAD MORNING.` → `A BOWL OF TEA AND A LITTLE BOOK.` → `EISAI.`

segments.voice: First, the journey. Eisai was trained as a monk in the Tendai school on Mount Hiei, the same mountain where Honen studied. He traveled to China looking for the living roots of the teaching, and there he received the Linji line of Chan. In Japanese, Linji is pronounced Rinzai. So the true person of no rank, from a few days ago, comes home with him. Tradition remembers Eisai as the one who brought Rinzai Zen to Japan. Second, the seeds. Tradition also says he carried tea seeds back from China and planted them, and that tea gardens grew from them. Whether every story about those seeds is exact, his love of tea is in his own words. Third, the book. He wrote a short work on drinking tea for health, the Kissa Yojoki. It opens by calling tea a wonderful medicine for nourishing life. For him, tea was medicine first, a way to keep the body well. It was practical, not decorative. Fourth, the pair. Eisai also wrote in defense of Zen, arguing that its practice could serve and protect the country. So he came home with two gifts that would, over time, grow into each other: a way of sitting, and a way of drinking a cup.
screen: `FROM MOUNT HIEI TO CHINA.` · `LINJI BECOMES RINZAI.` · `TEA SEEDS, AND A BOOK ON TEA.` · `TWO GIFTS: SITTING AND A CUP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the sitting half. Eisai came home with two gifts, a way of sitting and a cup. For now, just the sitting. Settle, and feel the weight of your body on the seat. Then check in with it the way a careful doctor might: the shoulders, the eyes, the belly, the throat. Is anything tired, tight or thirsty? Don't fix it yet. Just notice what the body is asking for, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
Eisai. The Japanese monk tradition remembers for bringing Rinzai Zen, and tea, home from China. Today's word.
Your line: tea and Zen. Today, before your next drink of anything, sit still for three breaths first. Then drink it as if it were medicine for the body. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

996.title: The old cook
996.hook: the young Dogen meets an old monastery cook drying mushrooms in the sun who won't let anyone else do it
996.howItsDone: In Soto Zen monasteries, Dogen's Instructions for the Cook guides the kitchen, and the tenzo prepares meals as a form of practice, with care for each ingredient and the people who will eat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eisai, who came home from China with a Zen lineage and, tradition says, tea seeds. Your line was tea and Zen. Did you make a cup slowly, step by step? Day nine hundred ninety-six.

Mushrooms, spread out to dry on a stone walkway at a Chinese monastery. The midday sun is fierce, and the stone is hot enough to feel through sandals. Out on it, bent over them, is the monastery's cook. He is old, his eyebrows white, no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, sweat running down his face. A young Japanese monk, visiting to study, stops and stares. Why is this old man doing this, now, himself? The young monk was Dogen, and he wrote the scene down years later. Today, tenzo.
screen: `A FIERCE MIDDAY SUN.` → `AN OLD COOK DRYING MUSHROOMS.` → `YOUNG DOGEN STOPS AND STARES.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The cook in a Zen monastery, the tenzo, was not a kitchen hand. It was a senior post, held by an experienced monk, because feeding the community was treated as practice of the highest seriousness. Dogen wrote a whole work about it, Instructions for the Cook, and this meeting is at its heart. Second, the question. Dogen asked the old man why he didn't have a helper or a worker do it. The cook answered, in Dogen's telling: others are not me. Your line comes from that. Not someone else. Third, the follow-up. Dogen pressed: fine, but why now, in the worst of the heat? The cook said: if not now, when? Dogen had no reply. He wrote that only then did he begin to understand what the cook's work really was. Fourth, what it means. The cook isn't refusing help out of pride. His practice is his own, and it happens in this hour, with these mushrooms. Handing it off, or putting it off until a better time, would be handing off his own life. For Dogen, who had come all the way to China looking for the teaching in scriptures and great halls, it was a surprise to find it on a hot walkway, in an old man's sweat. In this telling, the kitchen, the sink, even the inbox, are not interruptions to practice. They are the practice, and no one else can do yours.
screen: `THE TENZO: A SENIOR POST.` · `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · `NO ONE ELSE CAN DO YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the task that's yours. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing on today's list you've been hoping someone else will handle, or that you keep moving to later. A call, a dish, a form, an apology. Picture yourself doing it, plainly, in the heat of the day if need be. Notice any reasons that rise for not now. Hear them out, and set them on the counter. Then quietly say to yourself the cook's question: if not now, when? The bell holds the time.
Tenzo. The senior monastery cook's post, held by the old man who told young Dogen: others are not me, and if not now, when? Today's word.
Your line: not someone else. Today, do your own work, one task you'd usually hand off or put off, and do it now. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: Just sitting
997.hook: Dogen: just sit; sitting itself is awakening
997.carry: like a car passing outside the window
997.howItsDone: In Soto Zen temples and sitting groups, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, upright on a cushion, without counting the breath or working on a koan, and some groups recite Dogen's instructions on sitting together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenzo, the old cook, drying mushrooms in the hot sun, who wouldn't hand the job to anyone. Your line: not someone else. Which piece of work did you keep as your own? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

A young monk comes home to Japan from his studies in China, and people want to know what he brought back. Scrolls? Statues? Relics? In a talk recorded years later, Dogen says he came home empty-handed. All he had brought back, he said, was that the eyes are horizontal and the nose is vertical. It sounds like a joke, and maybe it is. But it points at the thing he spent the rest of his life teaching: nothing extra. No treasure hidden somewhere else. Just this face, this body, this cushion. Today's word is what he told people to do with it.

The word is shikantaza, a Japanese term usually rendered just sitting, or nothing but sitting. In a short text on how to sit, Dogen gives plain instructions. Find a quiet room. Sit on a thick cushion. Keep the body upright, neither leaning left nor right, forward nor back. Breathe quietly. Then, he says, let go of the whole wheel of thinking: don't judge thoughts good or bad, don't chase them, don't push them away. So far it sounds like a technique. Here's the turn. Dogen insists that this sitting is not a ladder you climb to reach awakening somewhere above it. In his teaching, practice and awakening are not two things. You don't sit in order to get enlightened later, the way you'd save money to buy a car. The sitting itself is awakening expressing itself, right now, in a body on a cushion. That's why he calls it just sitting. Nothing gets added: no counting, no picture, no question to solve, no goal held out in front. Dogen also passes on an old exchange. A monk asks a teacher what he thinks about while sitting so still. The teacher answers that he thinks of not-thinking. How do you think of not-thinking? The answer comes back: non-thinking. Thoughts are allowed to arrive and leave, and nobody grabs them. Soto Zen, which looks back to Dogen, keeps this kind of sitting at its center. On an ordinary Tuesday, it's the difference between waiting for a bus and simply sitting at the bus stop.
screen: `SHIKANTAZA: NOTHING BUT SITTING.` · `UPRIGHT, QUIET, LETTING THOUGHTS GO.` · `NOT A LADDER TO AWAKENING.` · `PRACTICE AND AWAKENING, NOT TWO.` · then, large: `THINK OF NOT-THINKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: just sitting. Let the body be upright, the way Dogen describes, not stiff, not slumped. Let the hands rest. Let the breath breathe itself; you don't need to count it. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a song, let it come and let it go, like a car passing outside the window. You don't need to follow it down the street. If you notice you've followed one, that noticing is fine too. Come back to the sitting. Nothing to get. Nothing to fix. Just this body, sitting here. The bell holds the time.
Shikantaza. Just sitting, nothing added, which Dogen taught is awakening itself rather than a road toward it. Today's word.

Your line: like a car passing outside the window. Today, the next time you sit down somewhere, a bus seat, a waiting room, a kitchen chair, take three breaths before you reach for your phone. Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

998.title: To study the self
998.hook: Dogen: to study the way is to study the self, to study the self is to forget the self (Genjokoan)
998.howItsDone: Zen students study the Genjokoan with teachers and in study groups, and some temples chant or read it aloud; teachers often point students back to it during sitting retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shikantaza, just sitting, with nothing added. Your line was like a car passing outside the window. Did you manage a few breaths on a bus seat or a kitchen chair before reaching for anything? Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Someone is sitting in a small boat, looking at the shore. The trees seem to be sliding past. The dock is drifting away. For a moment it really looks as if the land is moving. Then they glance down at the water against the hull, and it's obvious: the boat is the thing that moves. Dogen uses this picture in a short essay called Genjokoan. When we look out at the world with a confused idea of ourselves, he says, we get the movement backward. Today, the sentence he builds around that mistake.
screen: `THE SHORE SEEMS TO MOVE.` → `LOOK AT THE BOAT.` → `GENJOKOAN.`

segments.voice: Here is the heart of it, in plain words. Dogen writes, roughly: to study the Buddha way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be confirmed by all things. Take it one step at a time. First, to study the way is to study the self. The path isn't a subject out there, like geography. The thing you're studying is the one doing the studying: how your attention moves, what you grab, what you flinch from. Second, to study the self is to forget the self. This is the surprise. Look closely enough at the self and it stops being the solid thing at the center of everything. Forgetting here doesn't mean amnesia or self-hatred. It's closer to what happens when you're so absorbed in kneading bread or fixing a bike chain that the little narrator who comments on everything goes quiet. Third, to forget the self is to be confirmed by all things. Once the narrator steps back, the world isn't scenery sliding past you anymore. The dough, the chain, the sound of the street, they show up fully, and you're part of what's happening instead of watching it from a booth. That is the boat again. A self that thinks it's standing still while everything else moves has the picture upside down. Dogen goes on to say that even the traces of awakening are left behind and not held onto. Readers of the Genjokoan have worked on these lines for a long time, and they don't all read them the same way. But the sequence is clear on the page: study, forget, be confirmed.
screen: `STUDY THE WAY: STUDY THE SELF.` · `STUDY THE SELF: FORGET THE SELF.` · `FORGETTING: THE NARRATOR GOES QUIET.` · `FORGET THE SELF: ALL THINGS CONFIRM.` · then, large: `STUDY. FORGET. BE CONFIRMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: forget yourself in one task, and the task for the next few minutes is breathing. Sit comfortably. Feel the breath arrive at the nose, fill the chest, leave again. Each time the narrator starts up, how am I doing, is this working, what's next, notice it, and let the breath have your attention back. Don't fight the narrator. Just keep handing the attention to the breath, the way you'd hand a tool back to someone mid-job. See whether, for a breath or two, there's only breathing. The bell holds the time.
Genjokoan. Dogen's essay teaching that to study the way is to study the self, and to study the self is to forget it. Today's word.

Your line: forget the self. Today, choose one ordinary job, washing a pan, folding a shirt, writing an email, and give it so much attention that the commentator has nothing to say. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: Being-time
999.hook: Dogen: time isn't something you pass through; you are time
999.howItsDone: Zen students read Dogen's Uji with a teacher, slowly and often more than once, and bring its questions into zazen and into daily work in the temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Genjokoan: to study the self is to forget the self, and the boat that only looked like the shore was moving. Your line: forget the self. Which job swallowed the commentator? Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

Where did this morning go? We talk about time as if it were a river and we were standing on the bank, watching hours float away. We spend it, save it, waste it, kill it, run out of it. Time is the thing outside us, and we are the ones it happens to. Dogen wrote an essay that turns this around. Readers of Dogen explain that he took an ordinary Japanese word that means something like sometimes, or at a certain time, and read its two characters side by side: being, and time. Today, the word he made from that reading.
screen: `TIME AS A RIVER.` → `WE WATCH IT GO.` → `DOGEN TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: The essay is called Uji, being-time. Its claim, put plainly, is that time is not a container things sit inside. Things are time, and time is things. Dogen says, in effect, that the pine tree is time and the bamboo is time. Mountains are time, oceans are time. The person sitting here is time. Your life isn't something moving through the hours; this breath is the hour. He gives a picture. Say you cross a river and climb a mountain. Afterward it seems the river and the mountain are behind you now, gone, in the past, and you're up here in the present. Dogen says that's only one way of seeing it. The crossing and the climbing were being-time, fully, when they happened, and they don't simply vanish into a back room. In the same collection, in the Genjokoan, he writes about firewood and ash. We say firewood becomes ash. But Dogen says firewood has its own place as firewood, with a before and an after, and yet cut off from that before and after. Ash has its own place too. Each moment stands complete in its own position. Readers explain this essay in different ways. Some hear it as a teaching about impermanence turned inside out: nothing lasts, and so each moment is entire. Others hear a practical point for sitting: you can't be waiting for awakening later, because later isn't a separate place. Either way, the ordinary question changes. Not where did the time go, but what is this time being, right now?
screen: `UJI: BEING-TIME.` · `PINE IS TIME, BAMBOO IS TIME.` · `THE RIVER AND THE MOUNTAIN.` · `FIREWOOD HAS ITS PLACE, ASH HAS ITS PLACE.` · then, large: `THIS TIME IS YOUR LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: notice this moment as your life. Sit, and let the body settle. Feel the weight in the seat, the air on your skin. When the mind leans forward, toward later, toward after this, notice the lean. When it leans back, toward earlier, notice that too. Then come to this breath. Not a breath on the way to something. This breath, as the whole of what your life is doing right now. If it helps, say silently with the in-breath: this is time. With the out-breath: this is my life. The bell holds the time.
Being-time. Dogen's word, uji, for time and being as one thing: the pine, the mountain and you, not inside time but as time. Today's word.
Your line: you are time. Today, the next time you catch yourself saying I don't have time, pause for one breath and notice that you are, right then, time. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

not simply gone into the past

1000.title: Nichiren
1000.hook: the monk who taught chanting the Lotus Sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo
1000.howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists chant Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, called the daimoku, often morning and evening before a scroll called the Gohonzon, and recite passages from the Lotus Sutra; groups meet in homes and temples to chant together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, being-time: the pine is time, the mountain is time, and so are you. Your line: you are time. When you caught yourself short of time, did you stop for one breath? Day one thousand.

Day one thousand, and today a sound. In homes and community centers, people kneel or sit before a scroll and chant one phrase, steadily, again and again, a rolling rhythm that can fill a room: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. There are no long instructions to memorize, no complicated posture. Just a phrase, a voice, and a scroll. That chant goes back to a Japanese monk who said the title of one sutra held the whole of the Buddha's teaching. Today, Nichiren.
screen: `ONE PHRASE, CHANTED.` → `NAMU MYOHO RENGE KYO.` → `A MONK WHO PICKED A TITLE.`

segments.voice: Nichiren was a monk in Japan who studied widely and came to one conviction: the Lotus Sutra was the Buddha's highest teaching, and the way into it was its title. Tradition says he first chanted the phrase aloud at his home temple, facing the sunrise. Let's open the phrase. Namu means something like devotion, or I take refuge in. Myoho is the wonderful law, or mystic law, the truth the sutra teaches. Renge is the lotus flower, which grows out of mud and blooms clean. Kyo is sutra, a teaching. Myoho Renge Kyo is the sutra's title; namu is the devotion placed in front of it. Put together: devotion to the Lotus Sutra of the wonderful law. Why a title? In Nichiren's teaching, the title isn't a label on the outside of a book. It holds the whole sutra inside it, the way a seed holds a tree. So chanting the title is a way of meeting the entire teaching with your own voice, not only with your eyes or your intellect. That makes it a practice open to anyone, not only to scholar monks. Nichiren was outspoken. He wrote that Japan's troubles came from turning away from the Lotus, he argued hard with the schools of his day, and tradition remembers that he was sent into exile for it. Today his followers belong to several groups, including Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, and they differ on how to read his teaching and on who carries it forward. What they share is the chant. For Nichiren Buddhists, saying the title is not a warm-up for practice. It is the practice.
screen: `A MONK AND ONE SUTRA.` · `NAMU, MYOHO, RENGE, KYO.` · `THE TITLE HOLDS THE WHOLE.` · `SEVERAL GROUPS, ONE CHANT.` · then, large: `THE CHANT IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: chant the title three times, the way Nichiren Buddhists do. If saying it isn't right for you, simply listen to the sound of it in your head. Sit up. Take a breath. Then, at an easy, steady pace: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Again: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Once more: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Now let it go quiet. Feel what the sound leaves behind, in the chest, in the throat, in the room. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Nichiren. The Japanese monk who taught that the title of the Lotus Sutra, Myoho Renge Kyo, holds the whole teaching, and that chanting Namu Myoho Renge Kyo is the practice. Today's word.
Your line: the title of the Lotus. Today, notice one title, of a book, a song, a job, and ask what whole story it might be holding. Day one thousand.

1001.title: Ikkyu
1001.hook: the wild Zen poet-monk who mocked pomp
1001.howItsDone: Ikkyu is remembered in Japan through his poems, his calligraphy and folk stories, and Zen students and teachers read his verse as a reminder not to confuse the robes and ranks of practice with practice itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nichiren, and a whole sutra held in its title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Your line: the title of the Lotus. What title did you catch holding more than it seemed? Day one thousand one.

A Zen monk walks through town in shabby robes, and people say he drinks in taverns and writes poems that would make an abbot blush. He calls himself Crazy Cloud. Stories say that when his teacher offered him the certificate that proves a student's awakening, he wouldn't keep it. Another story has him at New Year, when everyone is celebrating, carrying a skull on a stick through the streets as a reminder. Not all of these tales can be checked. But they all point the same way. Today, the wild monk, Ikkyu.
screen: `SHABBY ROBES, TAVERN POEMS.` → `NO CERTIFICATE.` → `A SKULL AT NEW YEAR.`

segments.voice: Ikkyu was a Japanese Rinzai Zen monk and poet. His poems were gathered in a collection known in English as the Crazy Cloud Anthology, and through them, more than through any sermon, he is remembered. First, what he aimed at. In his poems Ikkyu jabs at monks who wear fine robes, collect titles, sell certificates of awakening and run temples like businesses. For him, all that ceremony could become a costume over an empty room. Zen was supposed to strip things down to the plain truth, and here it was dressing up. Second, how he aimed. Not with a treatise, but with laughter, scandal and verse. His poems talk openly about wine, love and the body, things a respectable monk was supposed to keep quiet about. Readers argue about how literally to take them. Some hear a monk refusing to pretend he's purer than he is. Others hear a teacher using shock the way a Zen master uses a shout, to knock a student loose. Third, the twist. Tradition says that late in life Ikkyu was asked to lead the temple of Daitokuji, the kind of place he'd mocked, and he took up the work of rebuilding it. The wild monk didn't drop out of the tradition. He kept loving it enough to laugh at it. And that brings this week together. Eisai's tea, the old cook in the sun, Dogen's just sitting, forgetting the self and being-time, Nichiren's chant, and now Ikkyu's laugh. Each is its own path, but side by side they share a small thread: meet what's here, without the extras.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: laugh at one pomposity, and let it be your own. Sit easily. Let a few breaths settle. Then bring to mind one small way you dress yourself up: a title you like to mention, an opinion you defend a bit too loudly, the version of yourself you post. Look at it kindly, the way Ikkyu might, from a tavern doorway. Let a smile come if it wants to. You don't have to throw the thing away. Just see the costume as a costume. Then rest in whatever is under it, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Ikkyu. The Japanese Zen poet-monk who called himself Crazy Cloud and used laughter and verse to puncture pomp. Today's word.
Your line: the wild monk. Today, when you notice someone, or yourself, puffing up, let a quiet smile be your whole response. Day one thousand one.
